canberra.title: Summernats hooks Canberra up with massive Aussie music line-up
canberra.snippet: Two massive nights of Aussie music’s going to light up Canberra as Summernats turns 39. The Veronicas, Birds of Tokyo, Playlunch, S...
canberra.content:
The Veronicas are just one of the headliners for Summernats 39. Photo: Supplied.

Two massive nights of Aussie music’s going to light up Canberra as Summernats turns 39.

The Veronicas, Birds of Tokyo, Playlunch, Sneaky Sound System and Mashd N Kutcher’s Anthems will all be performing their biggest hits and anthems.

Summernats co-owner Andy Lopez said the line-up would take the party to another level.

“On Friday night The Veronicas, Birds of Tokyo and Playlunch are rocking it out on the main stage, and then Saturday night is one huge party with Sneaky Sound System and Mashd N Kutcher’s Anthems show,” he said.

“It’s going to be a heap of fun.”

Millennials will be no strangers to the strings riffs to open The Veronicas’ ‘Untouched’ – an absolute banger that was recently voted the third-greatest Australian song of all time in triple j’s Hottest 100 of Australian Songs.

Twins Jess and Lisa Origliasso will also bring ‘4ever’, ‘Everything I’m Not’ and ‘You Ruin Me’ to Canberra as part of their massive catalogue.

Perth rockers Birds of Tokyo have spent more than a decade taking their massive anthems to some of the biggest stages in the country, from the AFL Grand Final and State of Origin to the Australian Formula 1 Grand Prix.

With a catalogue featuring ‘Plans’, ‘Lanterns’, ‘Good Lord’ and more, they’re built for big stages and huge crowds.

Bogan Funk creators Playlunch will take to the stage at Summernats 39. Photo: Supplied.

Rounding out Friday night is Playlunch, the self-proclaimed founders of Bogan Funk.

Summernats music fans won’t be messing with anyone’s trailers (à la Keith) as Playlunch bring their 90s nostalgia, retro dance music and unapologetic suburban swagger to the live act.

“We played Rockynats a few years ago, and it was an absolute ripper, proper chaos, exactly our vibe. So getting the call for Summernats felt like unfinished business, honestly,” Playlunch frontman Liam Bell said.

“Bogan Funk and burnouts, it just makes sense; we can’t really explain it better than that.

“Canberra, get your zinc on, we’re coming.”

Sneaky Sound System will take over Saturday with more than 20 years of disco, house and pop bangers, including ‘UFO’, ‘Pictures’ and ‘I Love It’.

Finally, Brisbane electronic duo Mashd N Kutcher will bring Saturday night home with their Anthems show.

With more than 1500 live shows under their belt and multiple platinum records, the guys will perform with a full live band playing huge tracks, throwbacks and dancefloor favourites in a massive festival set.

Their pandemic-era remix ‘Get on the Beers’ became a #12 Hottest 100 hit, while their ‘Will It Mash?’ series has built a huge following.

Mr Lopez said the music line-up was designed to crank up the party atmosphere across an already massive four days.

“I love that feeling when you roll through the gates and you know there are four days of absolute mayhem ahead,” he said.

“Thousands of awesome cars and beautiful people, crazy, cool stuff happening everywhere.”

Street Machine Summernats 39 takes over Exhibition Park in Canberra from 7 to 10 January 2027. Season Passes are on sale now, and one-day tickets go on sale later in the year.

canberra.title: Ex-ADF member accused of manufacturing firearms granted bail
canberra.snippet: A former member of the Australian Defence Force (ADF) accused of being linked to a major weapons-making operation has been granted bail a...
canberra.content:
25 August 2026

Dane Cameron Hobbs (left) leaves court with his lawyer Mitchell Greig after being granted bail. Photo: Albert McKnight.

A former member of the Australian Defence Force (ADF) accused of being linked to a major weapons-making operation has been granted bail after spending 19 days behind bars.

Police searched Dane Cameron Hobbs’ home in Taylor earlier in August 2026, where they allegedly discovered 3D-printed handguns and handgun parts, as well as about 30 3D-printed knuckle dusters, 12 tasers and seven cans of pepper spray.

Officers allegedly found weapons that had been packed into shipping bags, suggesting they were being prepared for sale and distribution.

When the 35-year-old faced the ACT Magistrates Court earlier this month, an officer said police believed “there is a larger scale manufacturing operation going on”.

While the court ordered a mental health report for Mr Hobbs, it was not finalised last week, so he did not return to apply for bail until Tuesday (25 August), which was still opposed by the prosecution.

His lawyer, Mitchell Greig of Hugo Law Group, said while there were concerns for his client’s mental health, it would be more beneficial for him to be in the community to deal with these issues.

Mr Greig said his client was on a pension because he had served in the defence force, although he currently couldn’t access it.

Magistrate James Lawton noted Mr Hobbs had no prior criminal history. He said due to the proposed bail conditions and the active role his parents would play in supporting him in the community, he would grant bail.

Mr Hobbs has already entered pleas of not guilty to one count of the unauthorised manufacture of a firearm and four counts of possessing a prohibited weapon without authorisation.

The matter will return to court in September.

canberra.title: PM to tell business leaders and the states there must be agreement over AI
canberra.snippet: Anthony Albanese is using his speech to the Business Council of Australia’s Annual Dinner on Tuesday evening (25 August) in Sydney to set...
canberra.content:
The Albanese Government ministry met in Perth on Tuesday ahead of the PM hosting National Cabinet in Sydney on Wednesday. WA Premier Roger Cook is seated to the right of the PM. Photo: Anthony Albanese Facebook.

Anthony Albanese is using his speech to the Business Council of Australia’s Annual Dinner on Tuesday evening (25 August) in Sydney to set the scene for Wednesday’s head-to-head with state governments over artificial intelligence.

The Prime Minister will stress that Australia has one chance to get AI policy right for the nation, and he is determined to take advantage of the opportunities the new technology offers while also ensuring the best laws are put in place to manage it.

Mr Albanese will host National Cabinet in Sydney on Wednesday, where some state and territory leaders will reemphasise their displeasure with the rollout of AI data centres and the expected surge in power use and environmental impact.

The National Cabinet meeting follows a meeting of the Federal Cabinet and full Albanese government ministry held in Perth on Tuesday.

Between the Federal Cabinet and the National Cabinet, the PM is unveiling more of his views on AI in his address to the BCA. It is his fifth consecutive attendance at the BCA annual dinner, which he has addressed each year since Labor won office.

This time, however, the Prime Minister appears to be talking to his state and territory counterparts as much as to the business sector when it comes to AI.

“AI adoption will continue to grow as business builds and tests newer capabilities, and frontier AI capabilities accelerate,” he will say.

“Australia can do more to unlock frontier AI development in Australia, and we must shape this change to harness the positive opportunities while minimising the downsides.

“Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential.

“That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained and locations are appropriate.

“Getting this right can ensure Australia is the infrastructure partner for our region … it will advance our national sovereignty, and it is essential for our national security, business productivity, science, innovation and resilience.”

At National Cabinet, the Prime Minister will seek agreement that AI represents a generational opportunity for Australia.

He will push for a national approach to support investment, share benefits and protect Australia’s interests.

Mr Albanese will outline that the Commonwealth will legislate nationally consistent minimum obligations for data centres. Those obligations for large data centres will focus on water and energy use, as well as location.

Laws yet to be formulated will seek to ensure that data centres don’t exert upward pressure on energy prices and that the firms behind them must make a positive contribution to Australia’s energy transition.

The large tech companies will have to use innovative approaches to water use to be efficient and sustainable, and to meet infrastructure costs.

And their impact on local communities must be minimal.

The legislation will also set conditions for AI training regarding copyright, security, safety and skills development.

The Prime Minister will stress that Commonwealth legislation will be designed to complement, not duplicate, state and territory planning and approval processes.

He will centre discussion at National Cabinet on National Standards for AI.

“The objective of all governments must be to turn our attractive investment settings into a comparative advantage that supports our national interests,” Mr Albanese will tell the BCA.

“Hosting large-scale AI training data centres, and unlocking frontier AI model training, will help Australia capture a larger share of the economic value, technical capability and strategic influence of AI – as well as boost the competitiveness of our start-ups and innovative businesses.

“We must establish conditions to attract investment in frontier AI training, ensuring AI is developed safely, securely, and in ways that respect copyright and provide control and payment to the creative sector.

“Every country is dealing with these enormous issues, just as I am sure every business in this room is considering the implications of this revolution.”

The latest forecast from the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) suggests power use in Australia will likely increase sevenfold over the next decade, due in large part to data centres.

“Electricity demand is growing through electrification, new industries and large loads such as data centres, while consumers are playing a more active role in the power system through CER (consumer energy resources), energy efficiency and demand flexibility,” the AEMO report states.

“At the same time, ageing coal-fired generation is retiring and being replaced by renewable generation, firming capacity and consumer resources.

“Maintaining reliability increasingly depends on the timely delivery of these new resources, and ongoing investment will be needed in new sources of electricity supply to ensure sufficient electricity production and peak capacity is available to meet consumer needs throughout the next 10 years.”

canberra.title: The Givers: Why CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer and Village Building Company CEO Rob Fisher give where they live
canberra.snippet: The Givers is a podcast series with Genevieve Jacobs exploring what motivates businesses to generously support ACT charities. Behind ever...
canberra.content:
25 August 2026

Start the conversation

The Givers is a podcast series with Genevieve Jacobs exploring what motivates businesses to generously support ACT charities.

Behind every charity is a business choosing to care. Listen to the people and companies quietly supporting Hands Across Canberra to empower hundreds of charities and help thousands of Canberra residents in need.

CDC Data Centres and the Village Building Company are both major commercial players. CDC straddles the booming tech world, while Village Building Company is a local fixture, providing many Canberrans with their homes. Between them, they’re driving significant sectors of the Canberra economy.

In both cases, community is also at the heart of their operations. CEOs Rob Fisher from Village and Greg Boorer from CDC speak in today’s episode of The Givers podcast about how strong community roots and a philosophy of giving shape their corporate culture and personal values.

canberra.title: Teacher fired for taking 3D-printed gun into high school to show to students
canberra.snippet: It was otherwise a normal day at a public Canberra high school when a long-term teacher waltzed into work with an illegal 3D-printed hand...
canberra.content:
The teacher was fired after she took this 3D-printed handgun into a school in April 2025. Photo: ACT Policing.

It was otherwise a normal day at a public Canberra high school when a long-term teacher waltzed into work with an illegal 3D-printed handgun she was planning to show to her students.

She took it into a staff room and revealed her dangerous creation to her supervisor – and even imitated the act of preparing to fire it.

One can only imagine what her supervisor must have thought.

“You can’t show that to students,” the supervisor said.

When the incident first caused a stir in the community last year, ACT Policing said officers believed it was “a misguided effort to demonstrate the capabilities of 3D-printing technology”.

Now, a recently published decision from the Fair Work Commission shows that the digital technology and maths teacher, who had 22 years’ experience, was fired for her actions.

Commission Sarah McKinnon said that on a weekend at the start of April 2025, the teacher printed a replica handgun with a 3D printer using plans downloaded from the internet.

Then on the morning of 7 April 2025, the teacher took the gun to school, walked into the Arts Faculty staffroom and proudly showed it to her supervisor, saying she intended to show it to her students.

The supervisor told her to put it back in her bag, and she did, but was apparently confused.

“What is the problem? What have I done wrong?” the teacher said.

Commissioner McKinnon said the teacher took the gun home after she finished work, although it had remained visible in her bag during the day.

The incident was reported to the school’s principal, who, in turn, went to the police before the teacher was suspended with pay and escorted off the premises.

The teacher made this 3D-printed handgun at her home before police seized it. Photo: ACT Policing.

Police soon went to her home and seized both the gun and her 3D printing equipment, while also issuing her with a formal caution.

Last September, through her lawyers, she said she brought the item to school with the intention of showing it to students if she received her supervisor’s approval. She wanted to introduce a 3D-printing course for students and intended to show them the item “as an example of the capabilities of 3D printing”.

She also said she “regrets her conduct” and made a written apology.

Commissioner McKinnon said the teacher, who is aged in her 50s, but whom Region has chosen not to name, had been employed from 2004 until January 2026 when the ACT Education Directorate fired her on the grounds of serious misconduct.

She then went to the Fair Work Commission, arguing her dismissal was unfair because it was disproportionate and harsh in the circumstances.

Commissioner McKinnon noted that the teacher’s actions were unlawful because the gun was a prohibited firearm, but accepted that there was no malice involved.

“Even so, the actions of printing a replica firearm and bringing it to school to show teenage students without realising that this was a bad idea were not simply misguided. They showed an astonishing lack of judgement for such an experienced teacher,” she said.

She also did not accept the teacher’s claim that she sought out her supervisor that morning to ask her permission to show the replica firearm to her students.

“This could not have been her purpose at the time, because it had not yet occurred to [the teacher] that there might be a problem with her plan,” the commissioner said.

“I find that [she] did intend to show the replica firearm to students.”

Commissioner McKinnon ultimately found the teacher had not been unfairly dismissed.

“ACT Education had a valid reason for dismissal and the process it followed in relation to the dismissal was a fair one,” she said.

The ACT Education Directorate was contacted for comment.

australia.title: Australia news live: Man arrested after allegedly attacking woman and boy in Melbourne CBD; Richmond denies players ‘making light’ of Swans scandal in footage
australia.snippet: Follow today’s news live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Number of NSW households in urgent need of priority...
australia.content:
Man arrested after allegedly stabbing woman with scissors and assaulting 10-year-old boy in Melbourne CBD

A man has been arrested after a boy and a woman were allegedly attacked in Melbourne’s CBD.

Victoria police said officers responded to reports of the attack at about 1pm after a 10-year-old boy from the Bass Coast region was allegedly punched in the upper body.

It is alleged that a 30-year-old woman from Cowes intervened and was allegedly stabbed in the upper body with a pair of scissors.

A 27-year-old man from Sunshine West was arrested at the scene, and police seized a pair of scissors. He remains in custody.

Authorities believe the alleged attacker and alleged victims were not known to one another.

Key events

    What we learned, Tuesday 25 August

  • 1h ago

  • 6h ago

  • 6h ago

  • 7h ago

    Australia needs 5,700 new donors of O-type blood

  • 8h ago

    Coles blames Ooshies for hurting its sales as it reports $1.09bn profit

  • 9h ago

    Aria bars ‘wholly AI-generated tracks’ from music charts, but allows tech in ‘supporting role’

  • 10h ago

    Jackson Pollock masterpiece Blue Poles to visit Perth

  • 11h ago

    Sydney trains fix expected to be hours away

  • 11h ago

    Welcome

What we learned, Tuesday 25 August

Achol Arok

That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today.

Before we go, these are some of the top headlines:

  • Urgent overhead wiring repairs saw major train cancellations and delays across multiple Sydney lines this morning.

  • The Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) has barred “wholly AI-generated tracks” from eligibility from its music charts, although recordings that use generative AI in a “supporting role” will be eligible.

  • Coles reported growing profit from its supermarkets despite a slump in alcohol sales and a delayed hit from Woolworths’ Disney “Ooshie” giveaways.

  • Lifeblood warned Australia needs thousands more regular donors of O-type blood in the coming week amid supply pressures, including seasonal illness.

  • NSW gaming rooms will be required to introduce facial-recognition technology when a statewide exclusion register is introduced in 2028 under new gambling reforms announced on Tuesday.

  • Embattled home builder Bathla Group has been placed into voluntary administration, leaving customers in limbo in what it says is a “perfect storm” of circumstances, AAP reports.

  • Tests have confirmed H5 bird flu in a second dead long-nosed fur seal found in South Australia.

  • A man has been arrested after allegedly punching a boy and stabbing a woman in Melbourne’s CBD.

  • Richmond Football Club has insisted a group of players filmed during the club’s Mad Monday celebrations were not mocking the recent Sydney Swans scandal, while the country pub that hosted the end-of-season gathering has attempted to play down the incident.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning.

Jack Larkin

Record August rainfall across South Australia

Heavy rain across South Australia has broken various records for the month of August, with minor flood warnings issued for the Onkaparinga and Bremer rivers.

Dean Narramore, a senior meterologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, said the weather system causing the downpour is expected to shift toward the east coast tomorrow and dissipate in the evening. When it arrives, heavier falls are predicted to take place west of the ranges in New South Wales and through the Darling Downs of Queensland. Narramore said:

It’s kind of that pattern where there’s lots of rain on and west of the ranges of New South Wales, but for the east coast, maybe only 1 to 5 millimetres around Sydney.

The BoM confirmed that several locations across South Australia broke the record for daily rainfall totals in August.

Richmond players ‘embarrassed’ over Mad Monday behaviour caught on video

Mike Hytner

Richmond Football Club has insisted a group of players filmed during the club’s Mad Monday celebrations were not mocking the recent Sydney Swans scandal, while the country pub that hosted the end-of-season gathering has attempted to play down the incident.

Video footage showed one player feigning shock as he was spanked on his backside by a teammate, while another appeared to whip a fellow player with a belt. A club statement read:

Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end of season gathering. The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour. The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters.

The Garfield Hotel, located 80km east of Melbourne, issued a statement earlier on Tuesday, saying the incident had been “blown out of all proportion” and that it “could not speak more highly” of the players’ behaviour. The statement read:

For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with.

They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that.

They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site. They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on.

It comes amid an ongoing Victoria police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at a Melbourne hotel where Swans players were staying last week. No one has been arrested or charged and the five Swans players separately suspended for breaching club standards have reportedly denied any criminal wrongdoing.

Mad Monday, the traditional end-of-season celebration for football clubs, offers players a chance to let their hair down but has over the years been criticised for being the catalyst for loutish behaviour.

Andrew Messenger

Qld LNP MPs laugh in response to parliamentary question about domestic violence

Queensland Liberal National party MPs have laughed at a question about the state’s domestic violence minister asking members of a victim’s working group to sign confidentiality agreements.

The Guardian reported last month that minister Amanda Camm had buried the findings of the group, and banned one member from contacting her office by phone.

The Labor MP Jonty Bush asked Camm about the Guardian’s report in question time, this morning.

She was made to ask the question twice, when government MPs broke out in laughter. She asked:

Speaker, the Guardian has reported that members of the domestic family and sexual violence working group were asked to sign confidentiality agreements. Does the minister stand by her director general’s estimates statement that members were not asked to sign NDAs?

Camm responded:

Victim survivors were asked to sign privacy forms, and that was in regards to other victim survivors, but they were not asked to sign NDAs.

The minister was later asked about media reports that service providers had been threatened with funding cuts for criticising the government.

She didn’t answer the question directly, but confirmed that she had cancelled contracts for some service providers. Camm said:

Yes, we have terminated contracts. Those people had no respect for taxpayers’ money. They had no respect for the child safety system of which they operated.

And they were allowed to get away with it, Mr Speaker, under those opposite (Labor).

Man arrested after allegedly stabbing woman with scissors and assaulting 10-year-old boy in Melbourne CBD

A man has been arrested after a boy and a woman were allegedly attacked in Melbourne’s CBD.

Victoria police said officers responded to reports of the attack at about 1pm after a 10-year-old boy from the Bass Coast region was allegedly punched in the upper body.

It is alleged that a 30-year-old woman from Cowes intervened and was allegedly stabbed in the upper body with a pair of scissors.

A 27-year-old man from Sunshine West was arrested at the scene, and police seized a pair of scissors. He remains in custody.

Authorities believe the alleged attacker and alleged victims were not known to one another.

WA to ban character references for all criminal cases

Criminals in the nation’s largest state will no longer be able to use good character references in court sentencing hearings in a bid to reduce their punishment, AAP reports.

The reform ensures sentencing focuses on the crime committed, not the offender’s reputation, Western Australia’s attorney general, Tony Buti, says.

Our decision to scrap good character references at sentencing hearings ensures that victims are always put first.

It is particularly pertinent to prevent victims of child sex abuse, sexual violence, and other offences from being re-traumatised, having to hear what a good bloke their offender is.

It also reduces the potential for inequality in sentencing where well-connected individuals receive an advantage because of their good character references, often written by friends, family and colleagues.

The reform will not prevent courts from considering relevant factors such as an offender’s prospects of rehabilitation, absence of prior convictions, or personal circumstances.

The move follows in footsteps of New South Wales, which introduced the nationwide-first reforms earlier this year.

Second long-nosed fur seal tests positive for H5 bird flu

Lisa Cox

Tests have confirmed H5 bird flu in a second dead long-nosed fur seal found in South Australia.

The seal, announced as a suspected case on Monday, was found at the Pages Islands, off Kangaroo Island. The South Australian government said testing by the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness had confirmed the result.

Authorities also detected three further suspected cases in birds on the Pages Islands: one little penguin, one silver gull and one Pacific gull.

It follows the detection of three mass mortality events involving more than 1,000 greater crested terns on the Pages Islands and at Troubridge Island last week.

The government said a magpie found at Robe on the Limestone coast was also suspected to have H5 bird flu.

Scientists fear the virus could soon spread to endangered Australian sea lion populations, with the Pages Islands home to one of the country’s largest breeding colonies.

Read more:

Andrew Messenger

Qld parliament unveils statue of state’s first female MP

A new statue of Queensland’s first female MP has been unveiled at the state’s parliament.

Irene Longman was elected in 1929, serving a single term as a Country and Progressive National Party MP for the seat of Bulimba in Brisbane.

Queensland’s parliamentary speaker, Pat Weir, who commissioned the statue, said Longman had faced challenges her male colleagues never had to worry about.

At the time, the building did not even have women’s toilets and Longman was denied access to the parliamentary dining room. As a result, the statue depicts her working on a speech at a small table, while having tea – on the veranda outside.

Weir said Longman had been responsible for genuine and substantial change, including the state’s first female police officers and the establishment of a separate children’s court. In a brief event to mark the occasion, he said:

The unveiling … celebrates the life and legacy of a remarkable Queensland pioneer whose vision extended far beyond social dimensions of this time.

Longman did not live to see Queensland get its second female MP (Vi Jordan, in 1966), its first female cabinet minister (Yvonne Chapman, in 1986), or its first female premier (Anna Bligh, in 2007).

Nick Visser

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will be your guide for the rest of the afternoon. Take care.

One Nation’s David Farley ‘needs to shut up’, George Christensen writes

Josh Butler

Former Coalition politician and One Nation member George Christensen claims new MP David Farley “needs to shut up”, accusing him of “freelancing on immigration” after further confusion on the party’s core policy.

Christensen, who quit the Nationals and later ran as a One Nation Senate candidate, said he had “played a small part in helping David Farley get elected”, including having “advised” Farley on messaging and media during his byelection campaign for Farrer – but says Farley runs the risk of “damaging” Pauline Hanson with his comments.

“David Farley repeatedly contradicts One Nation on immigration and leaves Pauline Hanson cleaning up the mess,” Christensen wrote in a blog on his Substack page.

It came after Farley on Sunday told the ABC’s Insiders program that One Nation’s immigration policy numbers would be “not too different” from Labor’s plan, forcing One Nation into damage control. It has also exposed growing confusion about Hanson’s immigration policy, with various members giving different ideas at different times.

Christensen said One Nation “does need to clear up the wording of its policy”, noting “confusion” between its written policy and Hanson’s media interviews. But he also criticised Farley over a number of departures from One Nation stances, including Farley saying he’d display the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags in his office, and voicing support for the Sydney Mardi Gras.

“For now, the most useful thing he could learn is when to shut up,” Christensen wrote.

australia.title: ‘Enough is enough’: 121 Indigenous Victorians have died by suicide in the past five years
australia.snippet: Royal commission recommended First Nations healing centres in 2021 but the Indigenous health service says the state has ‘done nothing’ to...
australia.content:
On the steps of Victorian parliament stood 121 empty chairs, marking the number of Indigenous lives lost to suicide in the state in the past five years.

All of these deaths, the state’s peak body for Aboriginal health said, came after the final report of the royal commission into mental health in March 2021.

Its key findings heavily emphasised Aboriginal self-determination, social and emotional wellbeing, and the establishment of two cultural healing centres.

The state government accepted all 65 recommendations from the final report and nine from the interim report, but is yet to fully implement those directly related to First Nations people who remain three times more likely to die by suicide.

The Victorian Aboriginal Health Organisation (VACCHO) chief executive, Jill Gallagher, said the tragic statistic showed that mainstream mental health services are not working for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

“A lot of recommendations came out of that report and not many Aboriginal recommendations have been implemented,” the Gunditjmara woman said. “The government has done nothing. We have not established those very important healing centres, and it is crucial to try and address those numbers.

“These aren’t just figures we’re talking about, these are members of our families. Our families suffer, our communities suffer.”

Gallagher said VACCHO had applied twice in the past five years to see the healing centres funded, with an estimated cost of $36.2m over four years.

Gunditjmara woman Nikki Foy, who lost her brother to suicide more than 20 years ago, said mainstream mental health services were not equipped to handle “complexities of the trauma that we carry”.

“We need healing centres that are culturally appropriate for our mob. Culture heals,” she said.

“Today, or tomorrow, some family out there will receive a phone call. A mother, a father, a brother, sister, uncle or aunty or grandparents will get that call and be told that their loved one has passed by suicide … enough is enough.

“We are the experts that know how to support and how to help our mob. Let us do that.”

Reducing rates of suicide in Indigenous communities is one of the 17 Closing the Gap targets.

Both the Victorian minister for mental health, Ingrid Stitt, and the opposition spokesperson, Emma Kealy, addressed reporters alongside Gallagher. But while both spoke of the need to address the self-harm crisis in Indigenous communities, neither committed to funding the centres.

The Coalition has vowed to repeal Victoria’s historic treaty laws and dismantle Gellung Warl, the representative body for First Nations Victorians set up within that treaty process, within 100 days if it wins the state election in November.

Asked if abolishing Gellung Warl would help reduce suicide rates, Kealy said the Coalition’s policy was focused on making sure Aboriginal community-controlled organisations were funded and said that “while the journey may be different”, the party was committed to closing the gap.

Stitt said she would continue to advocate “strongly within cabinet and within the budget process” to have the healing centre projects supported.

“Treaty is a huge part of this,” Stitt added.

“Proud First Nations peoples in Victoria have the solutions, and we will work really hard to make sure that they have the power to be able to deliver those solutions.”

australia.title: Man denied parole a second time over anti-Israel graffiti despite judge’s scathing critique of case
australia.snippet: NSW parole authority says Mohommed Farhat followed ‘extremist ideology of antisemitic character’ while separately judge ruled ‘Fuk Israel...
australia.content:
A Sydney man convicted of writing “Fuk Israel” on cars and setting another vehicle alight has had his release on parole rejected a second time, despite a supreme court judge stating the case appeared to be a “serious miscarriage of justice”.

Mohommed Farhat, 22, was initially due to be released on parole in December after serving 10 months in prison following the November 2024 vandalism in Woollahra.

But he remained behind bars after a rare intervention by the commissioner for corrective services, who then told the New South Wales parole authority at a hearing in March that Farhat’s offending showed support for “extremist” behaviour.

Last week, the supreme court justice Desmond Fagan delivered a scathing ruling after the state sought a supervision order for Farhat on his release from jail using the Terrorism Act.

Fagan found there was an “insignificant” risk that Farhat, who was of “limited intellect”, would commit a serious terrorism offence. He ruled the police, lower courts and various state agencies all incorrectly labelled Farhat’s actions antisemitic rather than “a curse against a foreign state”.

Fagan determined that Farhat, who has a Hezbollah tattoo on his neck, was treated more harshly than he should have been after he pleaded guilty to 15 offences in connection with property damage.

The judge accepted Farhat was paid to undertake the vandalism and said the case appeared to be a “serious miscarriage of justice”.

On Wednesday last week, Fagan said he planned to write to the commissioner for the state’s parole authority ahead of an expected decision on Farhat’s potential release following the March hearing.

The parole authority then handed down its decision on Monday, five months after the hearing. It did not consider Fagan’s findings or evidence that counter-terrorism police determined three weeks after Farhat was arrested that he was not ideologically motivated.

The authority’s decision to keep the 22-year-old in prison stated: “In the authority’s view, the offending was reflective of a deep-seated adherence on the part of the offender to an extremist ideology of an antisemitic character.”

The authority rejected Farhat’s explanation, accepted by Fagan, that he was paid to carry out the vandalism.

“Further, the authority does not accept the offender’s claimed ignorance of the meaning of the phrases which were used in the offending,” the parole authority wrote.

On Monday, the commissioner for corrective services, Gary McMahon, was questioned about Farhat’s case in budget estimates and his rare intervention in December, when he successfully applied to have Farhat’s parole order revoked without hearing from his lawyers. A fresh hearing date was then set for March.

People sentenced to less than three years in jail are typically released on parole when it comes due.

McMahon admitted in estimates he had not consulted with specialist police before making his arguments, which were accepted by the authority, that Farhat posed a terrorism risk and his offending was antisemitic.

Fagan said in last week’s decision it would be “unsound” for the commissioner not to consult specialist police. He found it would amount to “a serious failure of communication between agencies”.

“The conclusions of the counter-terrorism officers and the resolution of Strike Force Pearl were directly against an assessment that the defendant had exhibited religious or political radicalisation by his index offending,” Fagan said in his judgment.

McMahon acknowledged in budget estimates his intervention in Farhat’s parole decision was “uncommon” but that “the material that was before me at the time when I gave that consideration was that he did pose a significant risk to the community”.

The Greens MP Sue Higginson said in a statement she was “astounded at the lengths the state has gone to keep such a troubled young Lebanese Australian man behind bars”.

“Everyone from the NSW police, to the commissioner of corrective services, to the attorney general have circumvented the court process repeatedly to ensure someone with addiction, cognitive disability and ill mental health remains in custody,” she said.

A government spokesperson said last week the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, was “seeking urgent advice about the prospects of an appeal” over Fagan’s decision to knock back the state’s request for a one-year extended supervision order.

The application would have subjected Farhat to 55 conditions while living in the community when released from prison. That is now due in October, when he completes his full sentence with no parole.

The parole authority said in response to a question about why the determination was delayed after March’s hearing: “The determination for Mohommed Farhat has been handed down with reasons. No further comment will be made.”

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Woodside scraps clean energy targets; Sydney property developer collapses; and Japan’s moving castle
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Woodside Energy, Australia’s biggest oil and gas company, has scrapped its long-term emissions and clean energy targets, even after enjoying a period of windfall oil profits caused by the war on Iran.

As Jonathan Barrett reports, the energy giant is doubling down on fossil fuels after recording a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn ($A2.33bn) in the six-month reporting period, and is expecting even more financial gains by redirecting barrels of oil to markets willing to pay premium prices.

While Woodside is just one of a growing list of large oil companies amassing windfall profits, a recent run of deadly heatwaves in the northern hemisphere, made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels, has reignited calls for companies like Woodside to shoulder the growing environmental costs of rising temperatures.

Top news

  • Scots College trio who allegedly sexually assaulted teen girl have faced ‘repercussions’, judge says

  • ‘Petty grievances’ and an alleged troublemaker: unsealed Murdoch court documents give rare glimpse into bitter succession battle

  • Major Sydney property developer collapses after ‘perfect storm’, leaving buyers in limbo

  • Sydney shark attack survivor describes moment she came to face-to-face with ‘monster’

  • Ralph Carr, entertainment industry and AFL figure, sentenced to six years for ‘predatory’ rape of ex-staffer

  • eHarmony deceived Australian customers with ‘subscription traps’ that cost hundreds of dollars, court finds

In pictures

Woolworths’ latest Disney Ooshie collectibles have not only captivated Australian children, they have led to a short-term slump in competitor Coles’ sales, according to figures.

Ooshies, designed to fit on to the top of pens or pencils – in the shape of Disney, Marvel and Star Wars characters – have been popular with children who trade them at home or school in an attempt to collect all 40 characters.

But the collectible craze is not without controversy. Environmental groups are concerned about the volume of plastic that will eventually end up in landfill.

What they said …

“What many of us once feared has become a reality.” – Tim Winton

Author and environmental activist Tim Winton wrote in the Guardian about how the dangerous conditions climate scientists long warned of “have become our common”.

There’s nothing accidental or inadvertent about what we’re all suffering through together,” Winton wrote, “This is something that is being done to us. Knowingly. Which makes it a crime.”

Podcast

Burnham hands secret missile technology to Ukraine

Andy Burnham is making his first foreign visit as British prime minister to Ukraine, marking the country’s independence day.

Lucy Hough speaks to senior international correspondent Luke Harding about how Burnham will use the trip to pledge military support and diplomatic backing to Ukraine.

Listen to the episode here and watch on YouTube here.

Before bed read

After repairs to Hirosaki Castle in Aomori prefecture, officials employed a technique known as hikiya - whereby buildings are put on rollers and moved rather than dismantled – to shift the structure more than 2 metres. It took 1,800 people to drag the 360-tonne structure using ropes and rollers.

Daily word game

Today’s starter word is: LAST. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply.

Sign up

australia.title: Woodside scraps long-term emissions and clean energy targets despite windfall oil profits caused by Iran war
australia.snippet: Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn in the six-month reporting period Follow our A...
australia.content:
Woodside Energy has scrapped its long-term emissions and clean energy targets, even after enjoying a period of windfall oil gains caused by the Iran conflict, in a decision described by climate campaigners as “grossly negligent”.

Australia’s biggest oil and gas company recorded a 27% increase in sales profit to $1.67bn ($A2.33bn) in the six-month reporting period, according to financials lodged on Tuesday, after the price of crude surged amid disruptions to global supplies.

It expects more trading gains by redirecting barrels to markets paying premium prices for oil.

At the same time, the Perth-headquartered company said it would drop its commitment to invest $US5bn ($A7bn) in new energy products, such as hydrogen, by 2030.

It has placed its new ammonia business in the US under strategic review; an asset previously described as one of Woodside’s highest potential options for decarbonising power sources.

Under the new chief executive, Liz Westcott, Woodside is doubling down on fossil fuels while shifting the company further away from clean energy and decarbonisation targets.

Westcott told analysts on Tuesday the company would “retire” its so-called scope 3 investment and abatement targets, which refer to emissions produced by its customers, because the targets “were established in a different market context”.

“The reality is that markets for emerging lower carbon opportunities, including hydrogen, ammonia, and carbon capture and storage, have developed more slowly than anticipated,” Westcott said.

The company said that its new energy business would be guided by “customer demand and commercial markets”.

Emerging battleground

Woodside is one of a growing list of large oil companies amassing profits because of the Iran conflict at the same time as emissions-fuelled climate change affects communities around the world.

A recent run of deadly heatwaves in the northern hemisphere, made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels, has reignited calls for those same oil and gas companies to shoulder the growing environmental costs of rising temperatures.

Sophie McNeill, the Greens (WA) spokesperson on climate change, said Woodside had given up “any pretence of trying to reduce emissions”.

“Everything the climate scientists warned us about is happening, but all Woodside cares about is trying to make as much money while they still can, burning up our planet in the process,” McNeill said.

Brett Morgan, investor campaigns manager at climate activists Market Forces, said big polluters must be held accountable for environmental damage.

“Woodside has ditched its already feeble scope 3 emissions reduction and new energy investment targets, despite years of investor pressure demanding stronger climate action,” Morgan said.

He said major Woodside investors must respond by demanding an end to the company’s plan to expand fossil fuel operations.

A spokesperson for AustralianSuper, one of Woodside’s biggest shareholders, declined to comment on the Woodside changes to emissions and clean energy targets.

While Woodside has repeatedly said it supports the landmark 2015 Paris agreement to reduce emissions, its policies allow for the development of new fossil fuel reserves which it has argued are needed to fuel the energy transition to renewables.

It has also warned that protest groups risk choking crucial supplies required for energy security in Australia.

Woodside declined to respond to the criticism from climate groups on Tuesday.

Woodside’s plans to develop the Browse gasfields off the Kimberley coast are an emerging battleground between the oil and gas company and environmentalists.

The Conservation Council of Western Australia said Woodside’s decision to abandon its Scope 3 investment and emissions targets was “grossly negligent” and “a dereliction of its clean energy obligations”.

world.title: Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses
world.snippet: Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission The Duke of Sussex has stepped d...
world.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.

Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee of African Parks, which admitted last year that human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo.

The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.

In a 2024 report published by the Mail on Sunday newspaper, community members accused African Parks rangers of beating, waterboarding and raping locals to stop them from accessing their ancestral forests, which are now in a conservation area.

After the review, African Parks published a statement acknowledging that human rights abuses occurred in the Odzala-Kokoua national park, which it manages. It said that it had improved its safeguarding processes both at the park and institutionally.

A spokesperson for Harry said the duke, who was president of the charity for six years before he became a member of its board of directors in 2023, remained an active and avid supporter of African Parks.

“The duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said.

“His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”

Survival International, a global human rights charity that campaigns for the rights of Indigenous people, had called on Harry to step down as a member of the board.

Caroline Pearce, the executive director of Survival International, said it was “outrageous that for 10 years Prince Harry has served African Parks” while people working for it had “been responsible for abuse and violence against Indigenous people. His departure doesn’t undo that record — African Parks itself must now be held accountable, and must abandon this model of fortress conservation for good.”

Founded 26 years ago, African Parks manages more than 20m hectares (50m acres) in partnership with 13 African governments and hundreds of local communities.

African Parks expressed “deep gratitude” to the duke on concluding his tenure after his 10-year commitment to the organisation.

“His relationship with the organisation dates back to Malawi in July 2016, when he supported one of the largest elephant translocations in history. He served as president for six years before being appointed a member of the board of directors,” it said.

“Over the years, the duke has brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa. The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks’ work.”

The announcement comes as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are due to relocate to the UK from California with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

Former Suits star Meghan is said to be pursuing an acting role, with reports she has been in talks about a role in the third series of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix hit The Gentlemen, swiftly followed by other reports that the deal was off.

The couple are understood to be planning an “extended stay” in the UK, and their children are already enrolled in school, but it has not been confirmed for how long.

world.title: Video shows hundreds held captive after Nigeria mosque kidnapping
world.snippet: Gunmen ‌attacked worshippers in Dekara village on Friday taking women, children and older people An armed group has posted a video showin...
world.content:
An armed group has posted a video showing what ⁠residents said were about ⁠600 women, children and ​older people abducted in an attack on a mosque in Nigeria’s north-central Niger State last week.

The video, posted on Facebook and WhatsApp, ⁠showed large groups of people seated in a forested area surrounded by armed men. Several children could be heard crying in the background.

Mass kidnappings for ransom have become common in ⁠parts of north-western and north-central Nigeria, where heavily armed gangs frequently raid villages, schools and highways and hold them until ​paid large sums of money. The violence was previously focused in the north of the country, but gunmen have ‌increasingly moved south.

The video surfaced two days after the latest kidnapping, when gunmen ‌attacked worshippers at the mosque in Dekara village during Friday prayers, taking people away in what residents said were simultaneous raids on several communities.

In the video, a gunman speaking in Hausa addressed families of the captives and urged them to identify relatives among the people in the footage.

“These are all your people. We are showing you this video so that you can identify your family members, your fathers, mothers, children ‌and relatives,” the gunman said.

Reuters could not verify the exact date or the location where the video was filmed. However, no older version of the video was found posted ​online before Sunday.

Four residents said they were able to confirm the identities of some of those seized.

“The people in the video are from Dekara. I’ve identified 13 people that I know,” Ibrahim Abubakar said.

Another resident, Abdulmutallib Muqaddas Dindi, said those who appeared in the video had been seized during the prayers. “We have ⁠identified our elders, relatives, and some of us have seen their wives and children ​in the video,” he said.

Police ​and state authorities did not respond ​to requests for comment on Monday. Police had earlier confirmed an attack on worshippers in ​the area but said ‌they could not ​verify the number of people ​abducted.

Jamilu Ibrahim, another resident, appealed to the federal and state authorities to secure the release of the captives, pointing out the number of mothers with infants and children among those shown in the footage.

world.title: Children make up half of mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreads
world.snippet: West African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetected More than half...
world.content:
More than half of the mpox cases reported in Guinea-Bissau have been among children, local authorities have said, almost two months since the country announced an epidemic.

A national outbreak was declared on 4 July, just over a week after a 27-year-old woman became the first confirmed case of mpox in the west African country. Since then, there have been seven confirmed cases and 46 suspected cases. Half of those patients have been children, with 16 under the age of four.

In a statement on Thursday, Unicef warned that because the country’s health surveillance systems were fragile, the virus is probably spreading undetected, leaving even more children at risk.

Sandra Martins, the country’s deputy representative for Unicef, said: “This is the first time mpox cases have been reported in Guinea-Bissau, making even a small outbreak a major public health event.”

Mpox is an infectious viral disease that can be transmitted through close contact. There have been more than 2,000 mpox-related deaths among tens of thousands of cases recorded across east, central and west Africa since January 2024.

Health workers say the Clade variants are consistent with viruses circulating in neighbouring countries, meaning that a risk of cross‑border transmission in the region remains strong. The vast majority of confirmed cases are in the Bissau autonomous sector, where the capital is, while one case is in the nearby Biombo area. No deaths have been reported to date.

Dr Magda Robalo, a former health minister who led the country’s Covid-19 response, said that to eliminate the “biggest gaps in the health system right now”, increased surveillance would have to be prioritised and frontline capacity reinforced.

“Even though the numbers are small, new cases have appeared intermittently over several weeks, which means transmission is ongoing,” said Robalo, who is also co-founder of the Institute for Global Health and Development and former director of communicable diseases for the World Health Organization.

The outbreak comes as the country grapples with infrastructure challenges and the aftermath of the suspension of last November’s presidential election by the military, which remains in power. There was no electricity throughout Thursday in Bissau for instance because of petrol scarcity since the weekend.

Many public health laboratories in the region lack equipment to deal with epidemics but have institutional knowledge from handling other crises.

In Guinea-Bissau, that is no different but there is also a sense of urgency, with primary schools scheduled to reopen across the country in September. After the outbreak was declared, community health workers immediately began a door-to-door public awareness campaign with megaphones and translated leaflets, supported by the health ministry and international agencies.

These grassroots initiatives are seen as vital for building public trust in the public health sector. Earlier this year, the country suspended a controversial US-funded trial on hepatitis B vaccinations for newborns, citing ethical concerns and procedural flaws. The decision was lauded by many across the continent and has highlighted sensitivities around emergency health interventions.

world.title: Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says
world.snippet: Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state A ⁠landslide at a huge w...
world.content:
A ⁠landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to ⁠collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.

The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.

The landslide took ​place at about 2am (3am UK time) ‌in the Gbessia commune ‌of Conakry, according to a government statement.

The death toll was 30, with six ‌people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.

Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.

One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I ‌have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.

Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite ​reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a ⁠World Bank report published in April.

On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara​, announced ​that the government was closing ​the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to ​be relocated outside Conakry.

The prime ‌minister, Amadou Oury ​Bah, visited ​the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.

world.title: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal
world.snippet: Agreement is among largest third-country deportations driven by Trump administration’s immigration crackdown Twenty deportees from the Un...
world.content:
Twenty deportees from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement that will see the west African country receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The group arrived at the Roberts international airport outside the capital, Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements pursued by the administration since Trump returned to office last year.

The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberia’s justice minister, Natu Oswald Tweh, said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the west African country if they wished.

The US has agreed to extend visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months and pledged $124m in assistance as part of the arrangement.

Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that are not their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa. A new report by Refugees International and Human Rights First say the Trump administration has reached deals with at least 35 countries and has sent roughly 23,000 people to 26 of them as of early August, and makes the Liberia agreement the largest single arrangement so far.

Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.

In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

A February report by Senate foreign relations committee Democrats found the Trump administration had paid more than $32m to five governments, several with poor human rights records, to accept about 300 third-country deportees – including $1.1m per person to Rwanda for seven deportees, and $7.5m to Equatorial Guinea for 29, a sum exceeding all US aid to that country over the previous eight years.

The report found more than 80% of those sent to third countries had since returned home anyway, often at further cost to taxpayers, and cited cases where deportees with US court-ordered protections were removed to Ghana and Equatorial Guinea before being sent onward within days.

The state department disputed the report’s characterization of its enforcement record.

The Associated Press contributed reporting
